## Introduction

Spatial transcriptomics (ST) captures the molecular state of tissue at spatial
resolution — but biology is not static. Biopsies taken from the same patient
at different treatment time points (e.g., Baseline, Week 4, Response) reveal
*where* and *how much* molecular activity changes across tissue space. Standard
single-time-point analyses miss this temporal dimension entirely.

The **spatiotemporal extension** of `SFinxSDFA` adds:

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `make_st_synthetic()` | Generate multi-condition synthetic ST data for testing |
| `read_seurat_st()` | Import real Seurat objects (Visium, Xenium, MERFISH, Slide-seq) |
| `STFA_fit()` | Spatiotemporally varying coefficient GAM across conditions |
| `plot_stfa_static()` | Publication-ready faceted condition maps |
| `plot_stfa_interactive()` | Interactive HTML explorer with condition slider |
| `run_spatiotemporal()` | One-line pipeline orchestrator for pathologists |

This vignette walks through the complete workflow using **synthetic data** —
no Seurat installation is required.

---

## 1. Setup

```{r load-packages}
library(SFinxSDFA)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)
library(mgcv)

set.seed(42)
```

---

## 2. Synthetic Multi-Condition Data

`make_st_synthetic()` generates biologically realistic spatial data for three
clinical conditions. The pathway scores have a spatially structured gradient
that evolves across conditions — giving the model a real signal to fit.

```{r synthetic-data}
df <- make_st_synthetic(
  n_spots    = 150,
  conditions = c("Baseline", "Week4", "Response"),
  pathways   = c(
    "GOBP_REGULATION_OF_NEUTROPHIL_ACTIVATION",
    "HP_LUPUS_NEPHRITIS"
  ),
  seed = 42
)

# Inspect structure
str(df)
head(df[, 1:6])
```

```{r show-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  table(df$Condition),
  col.names = c("Condition", "Spots"),
  caption   = "Spots per condition"
)
```

The `Condition` column is already a factor, and an `images` attribute holds
placeholder matrices for histology overlays.

```{r check-images}
images <- attr(df, "images")
names(images)  # one entry per condition
```

---

## 3. Running the Full Pipeline

For most users — especially pathologists — a single call to
`run_spatiotemporal()` is all that is needed. It handles all steps
automatically and returns all outputs in one list.

```{r run-pipeline, fig.width=14, fig.height=5}
result <- run_spatiotemporal(
  data      = df,
  response  = "HP_LUPUS_NEPHRITIS",
  predictor = "GOBP_REGULATION_OF_NEUTROPHIL_ACTIVATION",
  k         = 8,    # spline basis dimension
  grid_n    = 25,   # prediction grid resolution (25 × 25)
  title     = "Lupus Nephritis Dynamics"
)
```

The result is a named list with four elements:

```{r result-names}
names(result)
```

---

## 4. Interpreting Static Maps

```{r static-plot, fig.width=14, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Spatially varying beta(s) coefficient per condition. White dots indicate spatial locations where the 95% CI excludes zero (statistically significant effect)."}
print(result$static_plot)
```

**How to read this figure:**

- Each panel shows the spatially varying coefficient β(s) for one condition.
- The **plasma colour scale** encodes β magnitude:
  - Warm colours (yellow/white) → strong positive association.
  - Cool colours (purple/black) → strong negative association or near zero.
- **White stipple overlay** marks spatial locations where the 95% confidence
  interval does not cross zero — i.e., the predictor pathway has a
  statistically significant local effect on the response pathway.
- Direct visual comparison across panels reveals *where* the pathway
  relationship strengthens or reverses during treatment.

Export at publication quality:

```{r save-static, eval=FALSE}
ggplot2::ggsave(
  filename = "Lupus_Nephritis_Dynamics_static.png",
  plot     = result$static_plot,
  width    = 14,
  height   = 5,
  dpi      = 300
)
```

---

## 5. Exploring Interactive Plots

### 5a. 2D Heatmap Slider

The interactive 2D explorer lets pathologists scrub through conditions using a
slider. The white dotted contour shows the significance boundary.

```{r interactive-2d}
# Already in result$interactive_plot — or build separately:
p2d <- plot_stfa_interactive(
  stfa_result = result$model_fit,
  title       = "Lupus Nephritis Dynamics",
  mode        = "2d"
)

# In an interactive session or RMarkdown HTML:
# print(p2d)
```

> **For pathologists:** Use the slider at the bottom of the plot to switch
> between Baseline, Week4, and Response. Regions where the white dotted
> outline appears are spatially significant. Watch how these regions shift
> across the treatment course.

### 5b. 3D Surface Explorer

The 3D surface shows the full topography of the β(s) surface — peaks indicate
where the predictor pathway has its strongest spatial effect on the response.

```{r interactive-3d}
p3d <- plot_stfa_interactive(
  stfa_result = result$model_fit,
  title       = "Lupus Nephritis Dynamics",
  mode        = "3d"
)

# print(p3d)
```

Save as standalone HTML files that can be opened in any browser — no R
required for viewing:

```{r save-interactive, eval=FALSE}
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(p2d, "Lupus_Dynamics_2D.html", selfcontained = TRUE)
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(p3d, "Lupus_Dynamics_3D.html", selfcontained = TRUE)
```

---

## 6. Inspecting the Fitted Model

The `model_fit` element contains the full `STFA_fit()` output, including the
fitted `bam` model object for advanced users.

```{r model-summary}
# Per-condition beta surfaces
cat("Conditions modelled:", result$model_fit$conditions, "\n")
cat("Grid dimensions:    ", dim(result$model_fit$beta_surfaces[["Baseline"]]), "\n")

# Range of beta values per condition
for (cond in result$model_fit$conditions) {
  brange <- range(result$model_fit$beta_surfaces[[cond]])
  cat(sprintf("  %s: beta in [%.3f, %.3f]\n", cond, brange[1], brange[2]))
}
```

```{r model-summary-full, eval=FALSE}
# Full GAM model summary (advanced)
summary(result$model_fit$model)
```

Significance across the tissue:

```{r sig-summary}
for (cond in result$model_fit$conditions) {
  sig_pct <- mean(result$model_fit$significance_masks[[cond]]) * 100
  cat(sprintf("  %s: %.1f%% of grid cells significant\n", cond, sig_pct))
}
```

---

## 7. Saving All Outputs at Once

Pass `output_dir` to `run_spatiotemporal()` to auto-save everything:

```{r save-all, eval=FALSE}
result <- run_spatiotemporal(
  data       = df,
  response   = "HP_LUPUS_NEPHRITIS",
  predictor  = "GOBP_REGULATION_OF_NEUTROPHIL_ACTIVATION",
  k          = 8,
  grid_n     = 25,
  title      = "Lupus_Nephritis_Dynamics",
  output_dir = "./SFinxSDFA_outputs"
)
# Saves:
#   ./SFinxSDFA_outputs/Lupus_Nephritis_Dynamics_static.png      (300 dpi)
#   ./SFinxSDFA_outputs/Lupus_Nephritis_Dynamics_interactive_2d.html
#   ./SFinxSDFA_outputs/Lupus_Nephritis_Dynamics_interactive_3d.html
```

---

## 8. Using Real Seurat Data

For real experiments, pass a named list of Seurat objects. The names become
the condition labels in all downstream analyses.

```{r seurat-example, eval=FALSE}
# Load your pre-processed Seurat objects (one per condition)
library(Seurat)

# seurat_baseline <- readRDS("baseline.rds")
# seurat_week4    <- readRDS("week4.rds")
# seurat_response <- readRDS("response.rds")

result_real <- run_spatiotemporal(
  seurat_list = list(
    Baseline = seurat_baseline,
    Week4    = seurat_week4,
    Response = seurat_response
  ),
  response    = "HP_LUPUS_NEPHRITIS",
  predictor   = "GOBP_REGULATION_OF_NEUTROPHIL_ACTIVATION",
  pathways    = c("HP_LUPUS_NEPHRITIS", "GOBP_REGULATION_OF_NEUTROPHIL_ACTIVATION"),
  k           = 12,
  grid_n      = 30,
  output_dir  = "./results",
  title       = "Real_Cohort_Analysis",
  # Optional: extract patient ID from metadata
  patient_col = "donor_id"
)
```

Supported platforms (all handled automatically by `read_seurat_st()`):

| Platform | Seurat object type | Coordinates extracted via |
|---|---|---|
| 10x Visium | `VisiumV1` / `VisiumV2` | `GetTissueCoordinates()` |
| Visium HD | `VisiumV2` | `GetTissueCoordinates()` |
| Xenium | `FOV` | `GetTissueCoordinates()` |
| MERFISH | `STARmap` | `GetTissueCoordinates()` |
| Slide-seq | `SlideSeq` | `GetTissueCoordinates()` |
